newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel to release portion of frozen PLO funds.
newsitem.headline: Israel to release portion of frozen PLO funds.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu decided on Monday to release a portion of financial transfers to the Palestinian Authority which Israel froze after a double suicide bombing, his office said.
An aide to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat welcomed the decision, calling it a "positive first step".

"The prime minister decided today in consultation with the foreign and defence ministers to release about 30 percent of the funds Israel held up and transfer it to the Palestinian Authority," a statement from Netanyahu's office said.

It said the decision followed "partial cooperation" by the Palestinian self-rule Authority in the investigation into the Jerusalem bombing, and swift Palestinian action in arresting and sentencing three Palestinians for the murder last week of an Israeli taxi driver in the West Bank town of Jericho.
The statement stressed that Israel was taking only a partial step in response to partial moves by the Palestinian Authority.
"Israel still expects strident Palestinian action in the war against the terrorist infrastructure, action that has still not been taken," it said.
The statement said Israel would continue its policy of easing sanctions against the Palestinian Authority in parallel with Palestinian security steps against "terrorism".

Israel clamped a security closure on the West Bank and Gaza Strip and froze millions of dollars in tax and customs transfers it owes the Authority under a 1994 economic protocol after two suicide bombers killed 14 people in the July 30 bombing.

Asked about the partial release of funds, Arafat aide Nabil Abu Rdaineh said: "It is a positive first step. We hope the Israeli government will lift the siege measures, including transfer of the remainder of the money owed."
Nasser al-Sarraj, director general of the Palestinian Trade Ministry, told Reuters: "Netanyahu and his government have no right at all to hold even one shekel."
The United States has criticised Netanyahu for freezing the financial transfers, calling the action counterproductive.
"We welcome any Israeli effort to reconcile the Palestinian economy's well-being with their own understandable concerns about security," a U.S. official said.

Israeli sources on Sunday expressed satisfaction at information it received from Palestinian security officials at a trilateral meeting including U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) representatives.

The sources said the Palestinians gave Israel the results of checks made on explosives found in early July in a West Bank apartment suspected of being a bomb factory of the anti-Israeli Hamas movement.
The Israelis said they needed to check the information against what they already had.
U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross spent four days in the region last week to arrange the trilateral security talks.
In a separate matter, Palestinian police on Saturday swiftly apprehended and tried three Palestinian car thieves who abducted and murdered an Israeli taxi driver.
Israeli government sources said on Sunday Netanyahu had sent an envoy to thank Arafat for cooperating in the case.
